messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The root cause of the bug stems from the way FastDateFormat's getDateInstance method caches instances keyed by style, timezone, and locale. When the locale argument is null, it is omitted from the cache key, but the method uses the then-current default locale (Locale.getDefault()) to create the FastDateFormat instance.

This approach leads to issues if the JVM default locale is changed subsequently because the cached FastDateFormat instance will have the old default locale embedded, but future calls with a null locale will not recreate a new formatter with the new default locale. Instead, they will reuse the cached formatter created with the previous default locale.

In the failing test, the sequence changes the default locale from US to Germany after some getDateInstance calls, expecting the FastDateFormat obtained afterward (with no explicit locale) to use the new default locale (Germany). However, due to the caching behavior, the formatter with the first default locale (US) is reused incorrectly.

The key problem is in these lines of FastDateFormat.getDateInstance(int style, TimeZone timeZone, Locale locale):

```java
if (locale == null) {
    locale = Locale.getDefault();
}
```

This locale value is only set after the cache lookup keyed by the locale parameter being null or not. If locale is null, null is excluded from the key, which means the cache key misses locale context, but an instance is created using the default locale at that moment. A subsequent change of the default locale does not cause cache invalidation, so outdated locale-based formatters are returned.

The test highlights this with formats format1 (locale Germany explicitly), format2 (locale null meaning default US initially), then the default locale changes to Germany and format3 is requested (locale null meaning now default Germany), and it expects format3 to have locale Germany, but caching returns the old US locale formatter.

This diagnosis aligns directly with the current bug report's description that FastDateFormat assumes Locale.getDefault() won't change, leading to wrong locale usage when Locale.getDefault() does change after caching.

Recent bug reports do not provide relevant information for this issue.

# Next, I would examine if the cache key creation can be improved or if a fix would require always inserting the Locale.getDefault() value as part of the key when locale is null, or a different design to avoid this stale-locale issue.
org.apache.commons.lang.time.FastDateFormat.getDateInstance(int, java.util.TimeZone, java.util.Locale)
